title: POC Weekly Caching Sync - Week 12
summary: Weekly check-in on prefix / KV caching work for the POC. Reviewed hit-rate numbers from last week's experiments, discussed normalization and prompt-reuse strategies, TTL tuning, and privacy/consistency trade-offs. Agreed on next benchmark run with canonicalization + 10s TTL bump for templates and a follow-up A/B to measure latency/cost impact. Action items assigned to both Redwood SE and Nimbus infra/ML team.
next_steps: Redwood to run canonicalization patch on staging and share updated hit-rate dashboard (Samir)
Nimbus to provide representative traffic sample and anonymized prompt templates (Alex)
Run 24-hour A/B benchmark comparing canonicalization + TTL tweaks vs baseline (Evan + Priya)
Schedule final POC results review in two weeks (Maya)
action_items: Samir (Redwood SE): Deploy prompt-key canonicalization to staging and update dashboard with KV/prefix hit rates by 2026-03-27
Alex (Nimbus ML): Share sanitized set of prompt templates and common prefixes by 2026-03-26
Priya (Nimbus Infra): Increase KV cache TTL for template keys to 30s in canary group and report any consistency anomalies by 2026-03-28
Maya (Redwood AE): Share pricing delta estimate for expected 20% increased cache hit rate by 2026-03-29
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Okay folks, thanks for joining, we have 45 minutes, agenda is quick: numbers, tuning, and next steps, right?
[00:22] Alex (Nimbus): Yep thanks Maya, we've been excited to see the preliminary hit rates but want to dig into the odd drop mid-day we saw.
[00:35] Samir (Redwood SE): Quick recap — last week we pushed the KV cache with prefixing enabled for templates and we saw baseline cache hits go from about 12% to about 31% on average across morning traffic, but afternoons dipped to about 17%.
[00:52] Priya (Nimbus Infra): Right the spike in cold-starts at 2pm when a bunch of batched jobs kick off, so unclear if it's TTL or key normalization.
[01:08] Evan (Redwood): We also noticed key entropy — some prompt templates include session IDs or timestamps embedded which kills reuse. That's where canonicalization helps.
[01:24] Jordan (Nimbus Product): To be clear, we do want high reuse for common customer-facing templates, but some of the longer exploratory prompts need full context and shouldn't be cached.
[01:40] Tara (Security): Quick flag about privacy — any canonicalization has to avoid stripping out PII; we need the sanitized flow and attestations.
[01:55] Samir: Totally. Our plan is functional — we canonicalize only the template structure, not user-provided variables; we'll hash variables separately and keep them out of the cache key. That's what we tried in the dev patch.
[02:12] Alex: In practice we saw the dev patch increase template hit rate to 55% for the top 10 templates, which was great, but the overall corpus only moved to ~35 because of long-tail prompts.
[02:29] Maya: Do we have a breakdown by intent? e.g., transactional vs exploratory?
[02:36] Alex: Yes transactional (payment confirmations, status checks) are very cacheable — they make up ~40% of calls and had 60% hit rate after canonicalization. Exploratory are 30% with ~10% hit.
[02:52] Priya: The afternoon dip correlates with batch jobs that include a variable JSON blob in the prompt; those are unique keys every time so the cache is cold.
[03:07] Samir: Two levers to consider: 1) more aggressive canonicalization to remove noisy fields, 2) TTL tuning for template keys to keep them warm across batch spikes. But TTL increases cause staleness for template-driven prompts when templates change frequently.
[03:25] Jordan: How frequent do templates change in Nimbus flows?
[03:29] Alex: Template churn is low; probably weekly updates for most, except A/B experiments that swap templates nightly in the product tests.
[03:38] Evan: So maybe use TTL separation: longer TTL for known-stable templates, short TTL or bypass for experimental templates. We can tag keys with a template-stability flag.
[03:50] Tara: That tagging also helps auditability for security. We need to log which variation served, and ensure logs don't contain PII.
[03:59] Samir: About metrics — we're tracking KV hits, prefix hits, effective latency improvement, and estimated cost-savings. Current numbers: baseline mean latency 280ms, with KV/prefix caching median token-time down to 210ms for cached calls.
[04:17] Alex: Cost side — preliminary guesstimate shows ~18% token cost reduction when template hit rates reach 50% because we avoid recomputing long context tokens.
[04:30] Priya: We observed one glitch where KV eviction after a burst caused a cascade of cold requests; we suspect the policy wasn't prioritizing heavy-hitter keys.
[04:44] Samir: We can adjust eviction policy to LRU with frequency weighting, meaning keep high-traffic prefixes longer. Also consider reserving a small hot-slab for known templates.
[04:58] Alex: That would help. Also curious about client-side normalization — should Nimbus preprocess prompts to reduce entropy?
[05:07] Evan: Client-side normalization is great because it reduces load on the server and makes keys smaller. But requires SDK changes — we can provide a small helper lib.
[05:18] Jordan: SDK changes are acceptable if low friction for product teams — can we get that in two weeks?
[05:24] Maya: Yes we can package small canonicalizer as a lib, but we need Nimbus to opt-in.
[05:30] Alex: We'll plan to opt-in for transactional flows first.
[05:34] Samir: On implementation details: canonicalization will replace user variable spans with placeholders, collapse whitespace, normalize punctuation, and lowercase where safe. We will keep a mapping for variables so we can re-inject on the response side.
[05:50] Tara: Make sure the mapping isn't stored in the cache key; it should be ephemeral and not logged.
[05:57] Evan: Agree. Also encryption at rest for KV entries is on by default in the POC private cluster, and we support KMS-managed keys.
[06:08] Priya: Good. Is there a way to tag whether a cache entry is derivative of a user-id so we can evict per-tenant?
[06:15] Samir: Yes we support namespace keys per-tenant; we purposely separate tenant namespace so eviction and TTL can be tenant-configurable.
[06:24] Alex: We ran a small A/B last night with canonicalization on 10% traffic: template hit rate up to 47% and tail latency improved by ~12ms median on cached requests, but overall P99 unchanged — still noisy due to those unique prompts.
[06:43] Maya: That aligns with expectations; cached requests help median but P99 needs other work like routing or model size for heavy queries.
[06:51] Jordan: For the POC success criteria we had: 1) 20-30% cost reduction target, 2) median latency under 230ms, 3) zero data-leak incidents. Are we on track?
[07:03] Samir: On track for median latency — with caching tweaks we hit ~210ms for cached; overall median currently 260ms so still a bit above target. Cost reduction potential looks like 15-22% depending on adoption. Security goal is met so far — no leaks.
[07:18] Priya: We'll need to measure per-route adoption to estimate true cost impact.
[07:23] Evan: Suggested experiment: increase template TTL from current 10s to 30s for a canary subset of keys and simultaneously enable more aggressive canonicalization for transactional flows. Measure hit-rate, median, and P99 over 24 hours.
[07:38] Alex: We'll be careful — don't want to stale an A/B template. We'll tag experimental templates to be excluded.
[07:44] Samir: Implementation notes — canonicalization patch is ready for staging, TTL is a config flag we can push to canary fleets. Also will add evict prioritization.
[07:56] Tara: We'll need the audit log sample for that canary; ensure logs are sanitized.
[08:01] Maya: Samir can you share the dashboard link after deploy?
[08:05] Samir: Yes will push dashboard and raw metrics to the shared drive. Expect link in the Slack channel.
[08:11] Jordan: On measurement, please include: KV hits, prefix hits, median latency, P95/P99, token spend delta, and per-template adoption.
[08:22] Samir: Will do. Also will include a breakdown of traffic classes (txn vs exploratory) as Alex requested.
[08:30] Alex: Another small ask — can Redwood provide sample pseudocode for client-side canonicalizer? That would accelerate SDK adoption.
[08:38] Evan: We'll include a lightweight JS/Python snippet.
[08:42] Priya: One more infra note — for the canary we want to reserve some GPU capacity so cold misses don't overload compute — can you suggest burst capacity config?
[08:52] Samir: Yes, we can configure burst to spin up extra pods and set a safe concurrency cap; we'll propose a config in the follow-up doc.
[09:02] Maya: Great. Let's recap next steps and owners.
[09:08] Alex: Quick question about pricing — if caching increases hits by 20% does Redwood adjust pricing or keep the same?
[09:15] Maya: Pricing guidance: hosted usage billing remains same per-token, but effective token spend reduces. For Dedicated/Reserved we can model economic offsets and show pricing delta for projected usage; I'll send a short pricing delta.
[09:29] Tara: And pls include security brief on canonicalization and sanitization.
[09:33] Maya: Yep.
[09:35] Samir: I'll push the staging patch this afternoon and share dashboard link by EOD tomorrow.
[09:41] Alex: We'll assemble sanitized prompts and send by Thursday.
[09:45] Maya: Great, meeting adjourned, thanks everyone.
recording_header: Date: 2026-03-24 10:00 UTC | Duration: 45 mins | Attendees: Maya Chen, Samir Patel, Evan Liu (Redwood) — Alex Romero, Priya Singh, Jordan Lee, Tara Collins (NimbusPay)
notes: Dashboard link to be posted in #poc-nimbus slack; Redwood to provide SDK snippets and canonicalization PR; Nimbus to provide sanitized templates and opt into transactional flows for client-side normalization.
